summary: Trickle is a simple algorithm that lets nodes in lossy, low-power networks share information efficiently. Nodes adjust how often they transmit: they spread news quickly when things change, and stay mostly quiet when everyone is consistent. It is a building block used by other protocols for low-power networks.

plainLanguage.summary: Trickle decides when a device should speak. When the devices around it all seem to agree, the device slows down and stays nearly silent. When it hears something that disagrees with what it holds, it speeds up and tells its neighbours, so new information spreads quickly without everyone shouting at once.

subtitle: A timer algorithm that makes nodes talk fast when data disagrees and almost not at all when it agrees.

tldr.problem: Nodes on a lossy shared medium, such as low-power wireless networks, need to keep data consistent without flooding the channel or wasting energy.
tldr.mechanism: A Trickle timer runs in intervals that double up to a maximum. A node transmits at a random point in the interval only if it has heard fewer than k consistent transmissions, and any inconsistency resets the interval to its minimum.
tldr.outcome: Nodes spread news within link-layer transmission times yet send only a few messages per hour when nothing changes. Protocols that use Trickle must define what counts as consistent.

today: RFC 6206 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2011. The metadata for this unit records no later RFC that obsoletes or updating it. The RFC describes the algorithm and the requirements for protocols that use it, and says it does not provide results about Trickle's performance or behavior.

sections.title: What Trickle Is For
sections.content:
The Trickle algorithm establishes a density-aware local communication primitive with an underlying consistency model that guides when a node transmits. When a node's data does not agree with its neighbours, that node communicates quickly to resolve the inconsistency, in milliseconds. When nodes agree, they slow their communication rate exponentially, so that nodes send packets very infrequently, for example a few packets per hour. Instead of flooding a network with packets, the algorithm controls the send rate so each node hears a small trickle of packets, just enough to stay consistent.

Because it relies only on local communication, such as broadcast or local multicast, Trickle handles network re-population, is robust to network transience, loss and disconnection, is simple to implement, and requires very little state. Current implementations use 4 to 11 bytes of RAM and are 50 to 200 lines of C code.

Trickle was originally designed for reprogramming protocols, where the data being shared is the code of the program being updated. Experience has shown it to be a mechanism that applies to a wide range of protocol design problems, including control traffic timing, multicast propagation and route discovery. The flexibility comes from being able to define, case by case, what constitutes agreement or an inconsistency.

The document describes the algorithm and provides guidelines for its use, and states requirements for protocol specifications that use Trickle. It does not provide results about Trickle's performance or behavior, and does not explain the algorithm's design in detail.
sections.plainLanguage: Many small devices share one radio channel and have very little battery. Trickle gives them a way to keep their information in step without talking all the time.

sections.title: The Basic Idea
sections.content:
Trickle's basic primitive is simple: every so often, a node transmits data unless it hears a few other transmissions whose data suggest its own transmission is redundant. Examples of such data include routing state, software update versions and the last heard multicast packet. This primitive lets Trickle scale to thousand-fold variations in network density, quickly propagate updates, distribute transmission load evenly, be robust to transient disconnections, handle network re-populations, and impose a very low maintenance overhead. One example use, routing beacons in the Collection Tree Protocol, requires sending on the order of a few packets per hour, yet the protocol can respond to topology changes in milliseconds.

Trickle sends all messages to a local communication address. The exact address used depends on the underlying IP protocol and on how the higher-layer protocol uses Trickle: in IPv6 it can be the link-local multicast address or another local multicast address, while in IPv4 it can be the broadcast address 255.255.255.255.

There are two possible results to a Trickle message: either every node that hears the message finds that the message data is consistent with its own state, or a recipient detects an inconsistency. Detection can come from an out-of-date node hearing something new, or from an updated node hearing something old. As long as every node communicates somehow, either by receiving or by transmitting, some node will detect the need for an update. If node A transmits that it has version V while B has version V+1, then B knows A needs an update, and the other way round as well.

The fact that Trickle communication can be either transmission or reception lets the algorithm operate in sparse as well as dense networks. A single disconnected node must transmit at the Trickle communication rate. In a lossless single-hop network of size n, the Trickle communication rate at each node equals the sum of the Trickle transmission rates across all nodes, and the algorithm balances the load so that each node's transmission rate is one nth of the communication rate. Sparser networks need more transmissions per node, but the utilization of a given broadcast domain, such as a radio channel over space or a shared medium, does not increase. That matters in wireless networks, where the channel is a valuable shared resource, and reducing transmissions in dense networks conserves system energy.
sections.plainLanguage:
A node transmits every so often unless it has heard a few other transmissions that show its own would be redundant. The data that matters depends on the protocol: routing state, software update versions or the last multicast packet received.

Because a node can learn by receiving as well as by sending, Trickle works in sparse and dense networks alike. A single disconnected node must transmit at the full Trickle communication rate. In a lossless single-hop network of n nodes, each node transmits one nth of that rate. Sparser networks send more per node without using more of the shared channel.

sections.title: The Three Settings
sections.content:
A Trickle timer runs for a defined interval and has three configuration parameters.

The minimum interval size, Imin, is defined in units of time such as milliseconds or seconds. A protocol might define the minimum interval as 100 milliseconds. The maximum interval size, Imax, is described as a number of doublings of the minimum interval size, the base-2 log of max over min. A protocol might define Imax as 16, which with a minimum interval of 100 ms gives 100 ms times 65,536, that is 6,553.6 seconds or approximately 109 minutes. The redundancy constant k is a natural number, an integer greater than zero.

Besides those three parameters, Trickle maintains three variables: I, the current interval size; t, a time within the current interval; and c, a counter.
sections.plainLanguage: Three numbers control the timer. Imin is the shortest gap between transmissions, Imax says how many times that gap may double, and k says how many neighbours must already agree before this node keeps quiet.

sections.title: The Six Rules
sections.content:
The algorithm has six rules. When it starts, it sets I to a value in the range from Imin to Imax, and begins the first interval. When an interval begins, Trickle resets the counter c to 0 and sets t to a random point in the interval, taken from the range from I/2 to I, that is, greater than or equal to I/2 and less than I. The interval ends at I.

Whenever Trickle hears a transmission that is consistent, it increments the counter c. At time t, Trickle transmits if and only if the counter c is less than the redundancy constant k. When the interval I expires, Trickle doubles the interval length; if the new length would be longer than the time specified by Imax, Trickle sets I to the time specified by Imax.

If Trickle hears a transmission that is inconsistent and I is greater than Imin, it resets the Trickle timer, setting I to Imin and starting a new interval as in the second rule. If I is already equal to Imin when an inconsistent transmission is heard, Trickle does nothing. Trickle can also reset its timer in response to external events.

The terms consistent, inconsistent and events are in quotes because their meaning depends on how a protocol uses Trickle.

The only time the algorithm transmits is at the fourth rule, so there is an inherent delay between detecting an inconsistency, which shrinks I to Imin, and responding to it, which happens at time t in the new interval. This is intentional: responding immediately can cause a broadcast storm where many nodes respond at once and in a synchronized fashion. By making responses follow the algorithm with the minimal interval size, a protocol can benefit from Trickle's suppression mechanism and scale across a huge range of node densities.
sections.plainLanguage: The timer starts short and doubles each time it runs out, so a quiet network settles into very rare transmissions. When something inconsistent arrives, the timer snaps back to its shortest setting, and the node transmits at a random point inside that short window rather than immediately, which keeps many nodes from firing at the same moment.

sections.title: What a Protocol Using Trickle Must Define
sections.content:
A protocol specification that uses Trickle MUST specify default values for Imin, Imax and k. Because link layers vary widely in their properties, the default value of Imin SHOULD be specified in terms of the worst-case latency of a link-layer transmission. A specification should say that the default value of Imin is four times the worst-case link-layer latency, and should not say that the default value of Imin is 500 milliseconds. Worst-case latency is approximately the time until the first link-layer transmission of the frame on an idle channel, and does not include backoff or virtual carrier sense.

The specification must also say what constitutes a consistent transmission, what constitutes an inconsistent transmission, what events, if any, besides inconsistent transmissions, reset the Trickle timer, what information a node transmits in Trickle messages, and what actions outside the algorithm the protocol takes, if any, when it detects an inconsistency.
sections.plainLanguage: Trickle is a building block, not a complete protocol. The protocol that uses it has to say what counts as agreement, what counts as disagreement, and how long the shortest interval is, in terms of the underlying link rather than a fixed number of milliseconds.

sections.title: What Happens When Nodes Disagree on Settings
sections.content:
It is RECOMMENDED that a protocol using Trickle include mechanisms to inform nodes of configuration parameters at runtime, but this is not always possible, and where nodes have different parameters Trickle may behave in unintended ways.

When nodes do not agree on the redundancy constant k, nodes with higher values of k transmit more often than nodes with lower values. In some cases this load is independent of density: in a network where all nodes but one have k=1 and that one node has k=2, the different node can end up transmitting on every interval, maintaining a Trickle communication rate of 2 with only itself. The danger is uneven transmission load that can deplete the energy of some nodes in a low-power network.

Mismatched Imin values are usually not a significant concern: some nodes transmit sooner after hearing inconsistent messages, but their intervals grow to a similar size within one slow interval time, and the suppression ends after that first slow interval. Mismatched Imax values cause long-term problems: nodes with small Imax transmit faster and suppress those with larger Imax, which are then always suppressed and never transmit, creating long-term inequities in energy cost.

Mismatched definitions are the serious case. If a receiver thinks a transmission is consistent but the transmitter would have thought it inconsistent, the receiver does not respond properly and inform the transmitter, and the network may never reach a consistent state. For that reason, unlike k, Imin and Imax, consistency definitions MUST be clearly stated in the protocol and SHOULD NOT be configured at runtime.

Section 6.5 covers the constant k. A protocol may wish to use Trickle with its suppression disabled, with k set to infinity, but in general this approach is highly dangerous and is NOT RECOMMENDED: every node will always send on every interval, which can lead to congestion in dense networks, and it is especially dangerous if many nodes reset their intervals at the same time. It is much more desirable to set k to a high value such as 5 or 10 than to infinity. Typical values for k are 1 to 5, which achieve a good balance between redundancy and low cost. If a protocol allows k to be dynamically configured, a value of 0 remains unused, and it is RECOMMENDED that protocols which need to turn off suppression reserve k=0 to mean k is infinite.

Section 6.6 notes that a protocol SHOULD set k and Imin such that Imin is at least two to three times as long as it takes to transmit k packets. Otherwise, if more than k nodes reset their intervals to Imin, the resulting communication leads to congestion and significant packet loss, and experimental results have shown that congestion losses reduce Trickle's efficiency. Section 6.7 urges protocol designers to suppress the instinct to tweak Trickle without a great deal of experimental evidence: further reductions in transmissions or response time come at the cost of failures in edge cases.
sections.plainLanguage: If some devices are set up differently from others, the ones with the smaller maximum interval can silence the others for good. The RFC therefore says the agreement rules must be the same everywhere, and only the timings may differ.

sections.title: Ways to Use Trickle
sections.content:
The algorithm has been used in a variety of protocols, in operational as well as academic settings, and the examples are not exhaustive.

For reliable flooding and dissemination, a protocol uses Trickle to periodically advertise the most recent data it has received, typically through a version number. An inconsistency occurs when a node hears a newer version number or receives new data, and a consistency occurs when a node hears an older or equal version number. When hearing an older version number, rather than resetting its own Trickle timer, the node sends an update; nodes with old version numbers that receive the update then reset their own timers, which leads to fast propagation of the new data. Examples of this use include multicast, network configuration, and installing new application programs.

For routing control traffic, a protocol uses Trickle to control when it sends beacons that contain routing state. An inconsistency occurs when the routing topology changes in a way that could lead to loops or significant stretch, for example when the routing layer detects a routing loop or when a node's routing cost changes significantly. Consistency occurs when the topology is operating well and delivering packets successfully. Using Trickle this way lets a routing protocol react very quickly to problems, with a small Imin, while sending very few beacons when the topology is stable. Examples include the IPv6 routing protocol for low-power and lossy networks, the Collection Tree Protocol, and some current commercial IPv6 routing layers.
sections.plainLanguage: Two patterns come up. A network that must distribute new data everywhere uses Trickle to spread it fast and then go quiet. A network that sends routing beacons uses Trickle to send them often while something looks wrong and very rarely when all is well.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As an algorithm, Trickle itself has no specific security considerations, but two security concerns can arise when it is used in a protocol. The first is that an adversary can force nodes to send many more packets than needed by forcing Trickle timer resets, and in low-power networks that increase in traffic can harm system lifetime. The second is that an adversary can prevent nodes from reaching consistency.

Protocols can prevent adversarial Trickle resets by carefully selecting what can cause a reset and protecting those events and messages with proper security mechanisms. For example, if a node can reset nearby Trickle timers by sending a certain packet, that packet should be authenticated so that an adversary cannot forge one.

An adversary can also prevent nodes from reaching consistency by suppressing transmissions with consistent messages. If node A detects an inconsistency and resets its Trickle timer, and an adversary can prevent A from sending messages that inform nearby nodes of the inconsistency, A may remain inconsistent indefinitely. Depending on the security model of the network, authenticated messages or a transitive notion of consistency can prevent this problem. To suppress A from notifying its neighbours, the adversary must send messages that are consistent with A, and those messages are by definition inconsistent with those of A's neighbours. Correspondingly, an adversary cannot simultaneously prevent A from notifying neighbours and not notify the neighbours itself, since Trickle operates on shared broadcast media. This means Trickle should filter unicast messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the timer reacts to what it hears, an attacker who can inject messages can make every device chatter, or can hide the news from some of them. The RFC's advice is to authenticate anything that can reset the timer, and to ignore unicast Trickle messages.
